passages.heading: Background
passages.text:
Through RI General Law §16-32-10 , academic responsibility at URI is delegated to the President and the Faculty Senate. With the President’s concurrence, the Faculty Senate has the authority to formulate policy concerning teaching and research, study, exercise, discipline, and government.
The Faculty Senate has oversight of the University Manual, which contains the rules and regulations that govern faculty and students. Additional oversight functions include curriculum approval, which provides for the establishment, abolition, and merger of programs, departments, courses, and curriculum, including general education.
To facilitate its charge, the Faculty Senate is composed of a six-member Executive Committee, six standing committees, and special committees as needed. Once elected to serve a three-year term, Senators are assigned to a Standing Committee based upon their interests. Senators may also serve on joint committees of the Faculty Senate and the President.

passages.heading: Annual Awards
passages.text:
The 2026 Service Award Winners were announced at the May 7, 2026 Faculty Senate meeting. Congratulations to Douglass Reed, winner of the Sheila Black Grubman Award, and to Furong Xu, winner of the Fritz Wenisch Award! Please join us in showing the gratitude of the URI community for their dedication, commitment, and service!
Professor Furong Xu’s record of service to the Curriculum and Academic Standards Committee (CASC) has been outstanding. Colleagues and fellow senators noted her skills in orchestrating a challenging committee workload, bringing disparate faculty members and departments together, providing steady leadership, and ensuring CASC was able to successfully navigate a record number of proposals in Academic Year 2025-26. CASC has been a remarkably productive committee this year, due in large part to Professor Xu’s smooth and skillful handling of ensuring the curriculum approval process operated in a timely and well-organized fashion. Additionally, faculty senators noted Furong’s steadfast collegiality, even-handedness, good humor, and grace. We congratulate Professor Furong Xu on winning the 2026 Fritz Wenisch Award for Exceptional Contributions to the Faculty Senate.

passages.heading: Annual Awards
passages.text: Professor Douglass Reed is the 2026 recipient of The Sheila Black Grubman Faculty Outstanding Service Award. This award recognizes a URI faculty member who has consistently dedicated their time, thought, and energy to make important contributions through service in the Faculty Senate, on committees, task forces, working groups, or other activities that promote the interests of the University and the URI community as a whole. As a Senator, Professor Reed was for many years a member of the Teaching, Advising, and Admissions Committee and was at the center of a major reimagining of academic advising. Many of the committee’s key recommendations are currently being implemented. More recently, Professor Reed has served for three semesters as the Administrator Evaluation Coordinator, adopting a mode of calm industriousness and a goal-oriented approach to this important work. Colleagues admire Professor Reed’s collegiality, work ethic, and practicality and we congratulate him this achievement!

passages.heading: Annual Awards
passages.text:
Since the Faculty Senate’s establishment in 1960 as the agent of the general faculty, elected Senators have served the Institution in matters of teaching, research, curriculum, academic standards and calendars, faculty status, and other systems as they affect the faculty as a whole. Senators value the opportunity to influence the practices and policies through shared governance with the President, University Leadership, and the Board of Trustees. They serve on standing, joint, and special committees as well as attend and participate fully in monthly Senate meetings. Faculty voices are essential to the success of an institution and necessary for academic freedom to flourish. Recognition of exemplary service to URI’s Faculty Senate through active and effective participation in the work of the Senate is made through resolutions, and annual and special awards.
The Sheila Black Grubman Award is an annual award established in 2011 and is awarded jointly by the Faculty Senate and the Office of the Provost to a faculty member who has made important contributions to and dedicated significant time and energy to the Senate.

passages.heading: Annual Awards
passages.text: The Fritz Wenisch Award for Exceptional Contributions to the Faculty Senate established in 2019 is awarded by the Faculty Senate annually to a Senator who demonstrates outstanding service.

passages.heading: URI Internal-Facing Survey Assistance (URI-IFSA)
passages.text:
The Faculty Senate recognizes that not everyone is trained in how to create and execute surveys. Nonetheless, even internal-facing surveys at URI should yield relevant and robust findings, and several URI faculty members have expertise in survey design/development. FSEC is creating a list of URI faculty trained in survey research who will volunteer to assist administrative and departmental offices, centers, institutes, unions, and other groups (henceforth referred to as survey organizers) to construct surveys as professional service to the university.
Where will the IFSA list reside?
The IFSA list will reside on the Faculty Senate website, which is openly accessible.
Who will manage the IFSA list?
Judy A. Van Wyk, Department of Sociology & Anthropology has agreed to construct/manage the IFSA list alongside the Faculty Senate Coordinator and apprise the FSEC Vice President about its status each January.
Who will be on the IFSA list?
The list will contain URI faculty members who volunteer to have their information posted on the list.
What will be on the IFSA list?

passages.heading: URI Internal-Facing Survey Assistance (URI-IFSA)
passages.text:
Every faculty member on the list must be willing to volunteer survey assistance. To volunteer, faculty will complete a short questionnaire .
Responses will be posted on the IFSA website.
Questions on the form include faculty name, contact information, areas of expertise in survey research, and their willingness to be contacted by other URI faculty for contracted or volunteered survey-related activities (which is not a requirement).
How will volunteers be selected to assist with surveys?
Survey organizers will access the IFSA list when assistance is needed, and they will select a faculty member from that list based on their areas of expertise they have listed in the questionnaire.
Survey organizers will contact faculty members directly via email or by phone. (If volunteers or survey organizers need assistance, contact Judy Van Wyk at vanwyk@uri.edu , or Lisa Bourbonnais at lbourbonnais@uri.edu .
Faculty are encouraged to respond to requests in a timely manner.
Do faculty members have to volunteer when they are contacted?
No. All faculty members are incredibly busy and may not be available when contacted.
What are volunteer tasks?

passages.heading: URI Internal-Facing Survey Assistance (URI-IFSA)
passages.text:
Specific tasks will be negotiated between faculty members and the survey organizers. The intention is to help/assist URI offices with professional survey development. Needs may vary, and the availability and expertise of faculty will vary.
Possible Examples
Faculty may meet with organizers before a survey is written to clarify the purpose and intent of the survey.
They may want to review survey drafts written by organizers and provide suggestions for revision, or they may wish to write the survey questions to be reviewed by the organizers.
Additional tasks may be negotiated and should be compensated by survey organizers.
Possible Examples
Faculty might input the survey for electronic administration in survey software or prepare paper formatting.
They may facilitate a focus group to test the survey instrument.
They may compile responses and create a database for the organizers.
They might analyze the data for the organizers and present their findings to them.

passages.heading: URI Internal-Facing Survey Assistance (URI-IFSA)
passages.text: Ethical guidelines : Survey organizers should be reassured, and faculty consultants should undertake, that work on a survey remains confidential and any discussions or draft language (even if not finally adopted) should never be shared, even after the survey period has passed.

passages.heading: Faculty Senate Executive Committee
passages.text:
Through RI General Law §16-32-10, academic responsibility at URI is delegated to the President and the Faculty Senate. The Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC) serves as the steering committee of the Senate. It represents the Senate in meetings with other University bodies and with the Provost, the President, and the URI Board of Trustees. Meetings of the FSEC are held weekly to coordinate the Senate’s business and its committees and address concerns within its jurisdiction.
For the description of the powers and duties of the Executive Committee, please see University Manual Appendix C: By-laws of the Faculty Senate, Section 4.1 – 4.9.

passages.heading: Joint Committee on Academic Program Review and Outcomes Assessment
passages.text: The committee is responsible for: (1) developing policies for URI student learning outcomes assessment, data distribution, and measurement frequency at the university-wide level, with the Faculty Senate’s and the Provost’s approval; (2) developing an ongoing review of the learning outcomes assessment process, interpreting external expectations for university-wide learning outcomes assessment, including those of accreditation bodies, and facilitating internal communication across units regarding way of meeting those expectations, and (3) guiding the implementation and revision of the Academic Program Review process (UM sections 8.86.10 – 8.86.14) and serves as a resource to departments and programs being reviewed. The committee shall also develop an ongoing review of the learning outcomes assessment process, interpret external expectations for university-wide learning outcomes assessment, including those of accreditation bodies and facilitate internal communication across units regarding ways of meeting those expectations. For more information, refer to Sections 5.84.10 – 5.84.14 of the University Manual.

passages.heading: Classroom Steering
passages.text: The Joint Classroom Steering Committee (JCSC) shall serve as a steering group to the functional areas that manage and have responsibility for classroom upkeep and planning (MTS, Enrollment Services, and Business Services). The committee shall be responsible for the development of plans for all aspects of classroom planning and management, including, but not limited to, the development and management of a single classroom data-base, the establishment and updating of design standards, scheduling and planning, assessment of needs for classroom refurbishments and setting priorities, maintenance and ongoing management of classrooms and the coordination of resources for classroom upkeep and improvement. This committee shall also monitor progress and the execution of these plans. This committee shall be comprised of representatives from enrollment services, instructional technology, space planning, business services, property, facilities, the university architect, the President, the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs, and at least three representatives of the faculty, one of whom shall be an academic department chair, appointed by the Faculty Senate. The chairperson shall be selected by the committee and confirmed by the Faculty Senate and the President. (University Manual 5.85.10 )

passages.heading: Online and Distance Learning
passages.text:
The purpose of the Joint Committee on Online and Distance Learning (JCODL) is to propose, examine, and recommend institutional policies and practices for developing, planning, and evaluating online and distance learning with a focus on quality, sustainability, and connection to the University’s mission, with approval of the Faculty Senate and Provost. Further, JCODL, considers faculty training, quality in delivery of online offerings, student learning outcomes, and ADA compliance regarding online and distance learning, as well as develops and implements strategic plans for online courses, certificate, and degree programs. (University Manual 5.78.10 – 5.78.11).

passages.heading: Centers and Institutes Review Committee
passages.text: The Centers and Institutes Review Committee (CIRC) shall review applications for Academic Institutes and Centers (AICs) and advance approved applications to the Faculty Senate for a vote prior to forwarding the application to the Vice President for Research and Economic Development and the Provost for final approval. The CIRC will also review applications for continuing authorization of centers and institutes, consistent with the four-year renewal cycle addressed in Section 8.90.30 of the University Manual. CIRC will also review and provide feedback on Academic Service Centers and Institutes (ASIC) because these typically serve the faculty’s needs. The Committee shall perform other duties as described in Sections 4.80 and 4.81 of the Faculty Senate By-Laws .

passages.heading: Space Allocation Committee
passages.text: The Space Allocation Committee (SAC) shall consider the present and future space needs of the University community, including new projects falling below the State’s Capital Improvement Plan project threshold. The committee will provide recommendations regarding space allocations requested to meet the programmatic needs of the University’s colleges and divisions. In making its recommendations, SAC shall consider future priorities of the University with respect to space, take into account the University’s academic priorities and strategic initiatives, and communicate with the Division of Research and Economic Development, the Campus Master Plan Review Team (5.40.10-5.40-13), the Joint Classroom Steering Committee (5.85.10-5.85.12), and the Strategic Budget and Planning Council (5.55.10 – 5.55.14) as needed. The Vice President of Administration and Finance shall review and approve space allocation recommendations prior to implementation.

passages.heading: University Manual Appendix C: By-Laws of the Faculty Senate, Section 4.28
passages.text: The Academic Calendar Committee shall comprise four or more members. The committee shall study the University Calendar for fall, winter, spring, and summer session semesters as prepared by Enrollment Services in accordance with University Manual passages 8.70.10 and 8.70.61, respectively, report it to the Faculty Senate by December 1; study the calendar for the fully-online accelerated program developed in accordance with University Manual passage 8.70.72 and present the calendar to the Faculty Senate by March 1 of the year preceding the one during which the calendar is to become effective; carry out all other functions assigned to it by University Manual passages 8.70.10-75; examine, cooperatively with the Graduate Council, such academic matters as may affect jointly the two committees; consider such calendar matters as may be referred to it by the Senate or its Executive Committee, and study, on its own accord, desirable changes in the University Calendar; review any proposed change in the approved calendar originating outside the committee as well as any amendments attached by the Faculty Senate to a calendar proposal prior to Faculty Senate adoption of the calendar in its final form except that, if the Senate Executive Committee declares an emergency situation prior to the Faculty Senate meeting at which calendar proposals are to be considered, a calendar proposal amended on the Senate floor may be approved at the meeting during which the proposal has first been introduced by the full committee. #17-18-12, #19-20-16, #20-21-14, #21-22-6, #21-22-37

passages.heading: University Manual Appendix C: By-Laws of the Faculty Senate, Section 4.40
passages.text: The Committee for Research and Creative Activities (henceforth referred to as the “full committee”) shall consist of six faculty senators and five non-senator research-active faculty) and students active, experienced, or concerned with various aspects of research, creative, and scholarly efforts at URI. The Vice President for Research and Economic Development (VPRED) shall be an ex officio (non-voting) member of the committee. The FSEC shall appoint six senators, and the VPRED shall appoint five research-active non- senators. #23-24-21

passages.heading: University Manual Appendix C: By-Laws of the Faculty Senate, Section 4.40
passages.text:
The full committee shall serve as the representative voice of the university community in all matters related to research, creative, and scholarly activities. It shall seek to improve the environment for research at URI in all ways possible. The Chair of the full committee shall serve as an ex-officio voting member of the Intellectual Property Committee (See University Manual section 5.30.10). The full committee shall form from its membership, a subcommittee, the Competitive Grants Subcommittee, the chair of which shall be appointed from the members of the full committee. The full committee shall meet at least once a month and present reports to the Faculty Senate in December and April and more often as needed. The Competitive Grants Subcommittee shall report to the Faculty Senate at least once annually. #17-18-18, #21-22-37 , #23-24-21, #24-25-19

passages.heading: University Manual Appendix C: By-Laws of the Faculty Senate, Section 4.70
passages.text: Constitution, By-laws, and University Manual Committee shall comprise four or more members. This committee shall review the operation of University governance and propose changes in the Constitution and By-Laws of the Faculty Senate and in the University Manual; review proposals for changes in University governance from whatever source and make recommendations concerning them to the Faculty Senate and to the other appropriate bodies and individuals; construe the meaning of the Constitution, the By-Laws and the University Manual upon the request of the Senate President or Executive Committee, any senator or member of the General Faculty, or the President; assure that all duly approved changes are incorporated into the Constitution and By-Laws and into the University Manual, and that no unauthorized changes are made in these instruments; and assure that the language of all duly approved changes is consistent with the style, format and arrangement of the Constitution and By-Laws and of the University Manual. #17-18-12 , #20-21-5 , #20-21-14, #20-21-36, #21-22-37

passages.heading: University Manual Appendix C: By-Laws of the Faculty Senate, Section 4.90
passages.text: The Budget and Administration Committee (BAC) shall comprise five faculty members, three of whom shall be faculty senators. The chair shall serve a two-year term and will be elected by the committee following input from the faculty senate executive committee. The Committee shall provide reports on their activities to the Faculty Senate at least annually and more often as directed by the FSEC or the Senate. Any specific BAC proposals for action will flow from the Committee to the FSEC and then to the Senate. #24-25-19

New Temporary & Permanent Course Email
The New Temporary & Permanent Course Email is distributed to all faculty, deans, and associate and assistant deans on the last weekday of each month. Recipients then have seven days to submit comments to the CASC Chair, GEC Chair, or Dean of the Graduate School regarding any potential or perceived content overlap involving a new temporary or permanent course.
The email serves two purposes:
Provides notice of upcoming Faculty Senate review. Courses included in the email have already been reviewed and approved by their respective College Curriculum Committees and will next be reviewed by the appropriate Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee: CASC, GEC, or Graduate Council.
Provides an opportunity to identify potential content overlap. College Curriculum Committees may review the courses included in the email to identify any potential or perceived overlap with courses offered or proposed by other colleges. Any concerns can then be raised before the courses proceed to Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee review.

passages.heading: Start the Proposal
passages.text:
From your browser, navigate to Kuali Curriculum Management (CM).
Select Curriculum to open your Dashboard .
Related toolkit entry: Dashboard
From the left-hand navigation menu, select Specializations.
On the Programs page, select + New Specialization in the upper-right corner.
The following sections of this walkthrough are grouped by section of the proposal form.

passages.heading: Contact Information
passages.text:
Complete the following fields with your contact information.
Proposer Name Your name is automatically populated based on your Kuali account.
Proposer Title Enter your university role.
Proposer Email Enter your URI email address. This is the email reviewers will use if they have questions about your proposal.
Additional Proposer(s) Use this section to identify additional individuals who can speak to the proposed program. Individuals listed here will not receive Kuali notifications or have access to edit the proposal. Their inclusion simply provides transparency to the reviewing committees about who else is involved in or can speak to the proposal.

passages.heading: Parent Program
passages.text: Inherit From Begin typing the name of the parent program, then select the program from the list.

passages.heading: Specialization Information
passages.text:
Effective Term & Year Select the term and year in which you intend the specialization to become effective. If the selected effective term has passed the applicable deadline by the time the proposal reaches the Faculty Senate, it will automatically be updated to the next available term.
First Graduation Term Select the term and year in which you anticipate the first students will graduate with this credential.
Level Select the level of the specialization: Undergraduate, Graduate, or Dual Dual applies to ABMs and 4+1 specializations.
🔽 The following field will appear only if Dual is chosen for Level.
Dual Type Refer to the linked pages above to understand the difference between ABMs & 4+1s
Academic Calendar Select the academic calendar for the specialization: Accelerated 7-week through URI Online, or Traditional 14-week with Summer and J-Term Sessions (must coincide with parent program).
College Select the college in which the program is housed.
Department Select the department in which the program is housed.

passages.heading: Specialization Information
passages.text:
Is this interdisciplinary? The intent of this question is to identify whether the parent program of this specialization is jointly owned by multiple academic departments. If yes, the percentage of ownership assigned to each department must be provided in the curriculum worksheet.
🔽 The following field will appear only if “Yes” is chosen for Is this interdisciplinary?
Additional Department(s) and College(s) Enter departments sharing ownership of this program.
Academic Specialization Title Enter the title of the specialization. See the linked page for title formatting guidelines.
Specialization Description List the requirements of the specialization. Only specialization-specific requirements should be listed here, and no program requirements should be duplicated.
Admission Requirements If the specialization has specific admission requirements, list them here. Otherwise, enter: “See admission requirements for {Program Title}.”
Total specialization credits (excluding program credits) Enter the number of credits required for this specialization.
🔽 The following field will appear only if ABM is chosen for Dual Type

passages.heading: Specialization Information
passages.text:
Total double-counted course credits Enter the number of credits double counted towards this ABM.
Attach Curriculum Worksheet
Upload a curriculum worksheet outlining the courses, credits, and other requirements that make up the proposed specialization’s curriculum within its parent program. You may use the University’s standard curriculum worksheets, or you may clearly include all requirements in a word document or PDF.

passages.heading: ABM Information
passages.text:
🔽 This section will only appear if the Dual Type is ABM.
Answer the following prompts:
List all bachelor’s degrees and majors eligible for application to this ABM program. Include any specializations (sub-plans or tracks).
Total earned credits at the time of ABM application (minimum 75)
Total earned credits required for admission (minimum 90)

passages.heading: Specialization Description
passages.text:
Specialization Description
Tags: specializations
Short Description: The University Catalog description of a program specialization, including its specialization-specific curriculum and any additional requirements for completion.
Specialization Description
The University Catalog description of the requirements for completing a specialization within an academic program, including the specialization-specific courses and credits required in addition to the program’s core requirements, as well as any additional specialization-specific requirements.

passages.heading: Specialization Description Formatting
passages.text:
Descriptive overview: A brief paragraph explaining the purpose and significance of the specialization.
Course Requirements
Important: Do not include program requirements in the specialization description.
Only include the requirements of the specialization in the specialization description, and exclude the core requirements to the program. The specialization
A specialization is an addition to the academic program, not a second listing of the program’s requirements. Students complete the requirements of the program and, where applicable, the additional requirements of their chosen specialization. The specialization description should therefore include only the requirements that are specific to that specialization.
Repeating the program requirements within the specialization could imply that students must complete those requirements again as part of the specialization. Keeping program-wide requirements in the program description and specialization-specific requirements in the specialization description makes it clear which requirements apply to the program as a whole and which are additional requirements for the specialization.
(For ABMs only) Courses that are able to be double-counted

passages.heading: Specialization Requirements
passages.text:
A minimum GPA average of 2.00 must be earned in the specialization courses (UM 8.20.61)
Half of the credits required for the specialization must be earned at URI (UM 8.20.61)
A maximum of one third of the total credits required for a master’s program may be double counted for an ABM program. (UM 8.30.19)

passages.heading: Topics Course
passages.text:
Topics Course
Tags: courses
Short Description: A course that allows different topics to be offered under the same course number.
Topics Course
Topics courses allow different topics to be offered under the same course number.
8.81.20 Open-ended Course. An Open-ended Course shall be administered by the department which originated it. Initially, an open-ended course shall be proposed and approved in the same manner as other permanent courses (8.81.10). Prior to offering a specific topic the content of the course shall be approved in a department meeting.
8.81.21 After approval of each offering of an open-ended course topic, a copy of the title, subtitle, and description shall be forwarded for schedule authorization to the Office of Enrollment Services via the dean of the college in which the department resides. The dean’s authorization shall ensure that no overlap exists between specific topics and existing courses.

passages.heading: Topics Course
passages.text: 8.81.22 A specific topic within an open-ended course may be offered three times. After three offerings the topic shall be approved through the appropriate channels as either a permanent course or as a permanent topic within an open-ended course and shall be included in the University Catalog.

Requisites are courses, conditions, or other requirements that determine whether a student is eligible to enroll in a course. Requisites may be required before enrollment, at the time of enrollment, or may establish other conditions for registration.
Common types of requisites include:
Prerequisites: Courses or requirements that must be completed before enrolling in the course.
Corequisites: Courses or requirements that must be completed concurrently with the course.
Other enrollment requirements: Additional conditions that may apply to enrollment, such as minimum class standing, program or major restrictions, or other eligibility requirements.
When entering requisites in Kuali, ensure that the requirements accurately reflect the conditions under which students should be permitted to enroll.

passages.heading: Track Your Proposal
passages.text:
Track Your Proposal
Track Your Proposal
Quick Links
Submitting a curricular proposal in Kuali begins a structured, multi-level review process, and we know you’re eager to know when your item will be reviewed and approved. While timelines vary across colleges, this guide will help you understand where your proposal is in the process and when to expect its full approval.

passages.heading: The Quick Version
passages.text:
For those who already know how the process works, but simply need directions on where to find the status:
Open the proposal in Kuali
Expand the workflow status

passages.heading: Step 1: Understand the approval path
passages.text:
All curricular proposals move through multiple levels of review. While this can vary slightly, most proposals follow this sequence:
Department-level review(s)
College Curriculum Committee
College Dean
Faculty Senate Curriculum Committees (Graduate Council, Curriculum & Standards, General Education)
Faculty Senate (courses are fully approved at this level)
University President (program modifications and new certificates, minors, and specializations are approved at this level)
Board of Trustees (new major and degree programs are approved at this level)
Each step depends on the successful approval at the previous level.
Check out The Approval Process for a flowchart and more detailed explanation of the approval process.

passages.heading: Step 2: Know the current proposal status
passages.text:
All who have access to Kuali have the ability to check on the status of every proposal currently under review. To find the current workflow status:
Open the proposal in Kuali.
Access it from your dashboard if you are the proposer, or
Search for it in the Proposals section, and use filters to refine results
Review the workflow status. At the top of the proposal page, the workflow status shows:
The current stage of approval
The users in the role of approving that step
Expand for full details. Clik the expand option to the right of “Workflow Status” to view:
The completed approval steps, and
The remaining steps before final approval.

passages.heading: Step 3: Know the submission deadlines
passages.text:
Department, college, and Faculty Senate committees each have deadlines for including proposals on their meeting agendas. Faculty should consult with their department or college curriculum committees for specific deadlines at those levels of approval.
Each summer, submission deadlines are set for college deans to help ensure proposals are approved by the Faculty Senate on a predictable timeline.

passages.heading: Deadlines By Proposal Item
passages.text:
Curriculum proposals must receive all required approvals by specific deadlines to take effect for their intended term. Deadlines vary by proposal type and may be influenced by registration dates, implementation requirements, and additional University approvals.

In some cases, new undergraduate courses, new undergraduate temporary courses, and undergraduate programs modifications may be reviewed by the Special Summer Curriculum Committee for a Fall effective date. Summer approval is not guaranteed and is considered on a case-by-case basis.
Unless otherwise noted, this does not apply to graduate proposals.

passages.heading: Step 4: Factor in Revisions
passages.text:
Many proposals require revisions during the review process. The following meeting results can impact your approval timeline:
Tabled: The committee needs additional information before making a decision. Once the requested information is provided, the proposal will be reviewed again at the next meeting.
Contingently Approved: The proposal is approved pending minor revisions or clarifications. No additional committee review is required. Once the conditions are met, the proposal will move to the next step.
Sent Back: The proposal requires substantial revisions. It must be updated and resubmitted, at which point it will re-enter the workflow from the beginning.

passages.heading: Step 5: Track Your Proposal Status
passages.text:
Proposal statuses can be tracked by logging into Kuali and expanding the workflow, or by searching for items that have been fully approved by the college in the proposal tracker.
2026-2027 Proposal Tracker
Please note: The proposal tracker is updated manually by the Faculty Senate Office and is not automated. While every effort is made to ensure accuracy, occasional errors may occur and are typically corrected after each Faculty Senate meeting. For the most up-to-date status, please check Kuali.

passages.heading: Step 6: Final Check
passages.text:
By the Monday prior to each monthly Faculty Senate meeting, the Faculty Senate Office distributes the Senate agenda to all faculty.
This agenda includes reports from the Graduate Council, Curriculum & Standards Committee, and General Education Committee, which are voted on during the meeting.
If your proposal has been approved by a committee but does not appear on the agenda, please contact the committee chair or the Faculty Senate Office. Reports are prepared manually, and with a high volume of proposals each month, occasional errors may occur. These are typically resolved quickly.

passages.heading: Course Proposals after the Senate Meeting
passages.text: The integration between Kuali and PeopleSoft is not immediate, can take several days, and requires review by Enrollment Services to ensure all information migrated accurately. Please allow up to two weeks after the Senate Meeting for new courses and course modifications to appear in eCampus.

passages.heading: Program Proposals after the Senate Meeting
passages.text:
Once curriculum committee reports are approved by the Faculty Senate, they are converted into Bills. Bills are signed by the Faculty Senate President and forwarded to the University President for review and signature. Once the University President signs & approves, the Bills are returned to the Faculty Senate Office and the proposals are approved in Kuali.
Special Case: New Majors and New Degree Programs
After University President approval, these proposals are forwarded to the Board of Trustees. Once the Faculty Senate Office confirms Board approval, the new major or degree is fully approved in Kuali.
The URI Board of Trustees meeting dates can be found here.

passages.heading: What is the Curriculum Toolkit?
passages.text:
This toolkit helps faculty, committees, chairs, deans, and other stakeholders create, review, and advance curriculum proposals through the University’s approval process. It outlines roles, expectations, processes, and resources to support accurate, efficient proposals and effective shared governance.
The Playbook focuses on process, not content. Faculty remain the subject-matter experts on academic purpose, curriculum, and learning outcomes; this resource provides the framework for moving proposals smoothly through review and approval.
It is designed so that everyone can start where they need help without having to sort through guidance intended for other roles.

New Temporary & Permanent Course Email
The New Temporary & Permanent Course Email is distributed to all faculty, deans, and associate and assistant deans on the last weekday of each month. Recipients then have seven days to submit comments to the CASC Chair, GEC Chair, or Dean of the Graduate School regarding any potential or perceived content overlap involving a new temporary or permanent course.
The email serves two purposes:
Provides notice of upcoming Faculty Senate review. Courses included in the email have already been reviewed and approved by their respective College Curriculum Committees and will next be reviewed by the appropriate Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee: CASC, GEC, or Graduate Council.
Provides an opportunity to identify potential content overlap. College Curriculum Committees may review the courses included in the email to identify any potential or perceived overlap with courses offered or proposed by other colleges. Any concerns can then be raised before the courses proceed to Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee review.

passages.heading: Choosing the Right Proposal Type
passages.text:
Choosing the Right Proposal Type
Choosing the Right Proposal Type
Course Proposal Types
There are two types of curricular proposals: modifying an existing curricular item or creating a new one. Selecting the correct proposal type is important. Proposals submitted under the wrong category will be denied and must be resubmitted.
Course modifications that are sometimes mistaken for new courses include:
Making a temporary course permanent
Changing the subject code of an existing course
Adding a new cross-listing to an existing course
A new course proposal is appropriate for:
Creating a new permanent course
Creating a new temporary course
Program Proposal Types
There are two types of curricular proposals: modifying an existing curricular item or creating a new one. It is important to select the correct proposal type, as proposals submitted under the wrong category will be denied and must be resubmitted.

passages.heading: Program Credential Types
passages.text:
In addition to selecting the appropriate proposal type, each program is classified under one of four credential types: Degree, Major, Certificate, or Minor. The credential type identifies the type of academic program being proposed.
Degree
An academic credential awarded by the University upon successful completion of a prescribed program of study. Degrees include bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees.
In Kuali, select Degree when the program is the only program offered under that degree. Examples include the MPS (Master of Professional Studies), BIS (Bachelor of Interdisciplinary Studies), Pharm.D. (Doctor of Pharmacy), and DNP (Doctor of Nursing Practice).
Major
A defined field of study within a degree program consisting of a required set of courses and related academic requirements in a specific discipline.
In Kuali, select Major when the program is one of multiple options offered under the same degree. These typically include BA, BS, MA, MS, and PhD programs.
Certificate
A formal program of study consisting of a defined set of courses in a focused area. Certificates may be completed independently or in conjunction with a degree program.
Minor

passages.heading: Program Credential Types
passages.text:
A secondary field of study consisting of a prescribed set of courses in a discipline outside a student’s major. A minor is intended to complement a student’s primary area of study.
Specialization Proposal Types
There are two types of curricular proposals: modifying an existing curricular item or creating a new one. It is important to select the correct proposal type, as proposals submitted under the wrong category will be denied and must be resubmitted.

passages.heading: 🚨 Understanding Specializations, Sub-Plans, Options, Tracks, Focus Areas, and Concentrations
passages.text: At URI, these terms refer to different curricular structures. Understanding how they differ is essential to ensure that programs and their areas of study are proposed and documented correctly.

passages.heading: Specializations, Sub-Plans, Options, and Tracks
passages.text:
These represent a formally recognized area of study within a program. They:
Are coded in eCampus
Have defined requirements that students must complete
Appear on the student’s transcript
Are formally created and maintained through the Specializations section of Kuali
Note: The terminology used may vary by system or University Manual terminology. For curricular proposal purposes, these structures are treated as specializations in Kuali.

passages.heading: Concentrations and Focus Areas
passages.text:
These represent an optional area of study within a program. They:
Are not coded in eCampus
May include suggested courses or course sequences to guide students
Do not appear on the student’s transcript
Are described within the program description to which they belong
Do not require a separate curricular proposal

passages.heading: What about ABMs and “4 + 1” Programs?
passages.text:
Both Accelerated Bachelor’s to Master’s (ABM) programs and “4 + 1” programs are formally recognized Specializations, but they differ in how they are structured and which degree program they belong to.
ABM Specializations
Are inherited by the Master’s degree
Identify a defined pathway from the Bachelor’s degree into the Master’s degree
Include an identified set of courses that may be double-counted toward both the Bachelor’s and Master’s degree requirements
“4 + 1” Specializations
Are inherited by the Bachelor’s degree
Do not include courses that are double-counted toward both degrees
Provide guidance on courses students should take during the final semesters of their undergraduate degree to help shorten the time needed to complete the Master’s degree

passages.heading: Letter Grades

A grading method in which student performance is evaluated using letter grades from A (Superior) through F (Failure), with each grade assigned a quality point value used to calculate GPA.
8.53.10 Student grades are defined as follows: A – Superior B – Good C – Fair D – Low grade, passing F – Failure 8.53.11 Grades shall be given quality point values as follows: A = 4.00 points A- = 3.70 points B+ = 3.30 points B = 3.00 points B- = 2.70 points C+ = 2.30 points C = 2.00 points C- = 1.70 points D+ = 1.30 points D = 1.00 points F = 0 points U = 0 points U* = not calculated in GPA

passages.heading: New Temporary & Permanent Course Email
passages.text:
New Temporary & Permanent Course Email
Date: December 31, 2026 (2026-12-31)
Tags: Temp Course Email
New Temporary & Permanent Course Email
The New Temporary & Permanent Course Email is distributed to all faculty, deans, and associate and assistant deans on the last weekday of each month. Recipients then have seven days to submit comments to the CASC Chair, GEC Chair, or Dean of the Graduate School regarding any potential or perceived content overlap involving a new temporary or permanent course.
The email serves two purposes:
Provides notice of upcoming Faculty Senate review. Courses included in the email have already been reviewed and approved by their respective College Curriculum Committees and will next be reviewed by the appropriate Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee: CASC, GEC, or Graduate Council.
Provides an opportunity to identify potential content overlap. College Curriculum Committees may review the courses included in the email to identify any potential or perceived overlap with courses offered or proposed by other colleges. Any concerns can then be raised before the courses proceed to Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee review.

passages.heading: Instructional Delivery Method
passages.text:
Instructional Delivery Method
Tags: courses
Short Description: The instructional delivery method. Also known as "method of instruction.”
Instructional Delivery Method
Provided below is the complete list of approved methods of instruction, as proposed in FSEC Report #2024-2025-03 and subsequently approved by the Faculty Senate through Bill #24-25-12 on January 23, 2025.

passages.heading: Lecture
passages.text: A course in which the primary method is presentation and students are expected to participate in a variety of ways, such as small-group discussions, questions and answers, writing-exercises, etc.

passages.heading: Laboratory
passages.text: Applied course work, generally involving experimentation or observation, typically using special equipment (including computers and specialized software).

passages.heading: Recitation
passages.text: Separate sections of a lecture course regularly scheduled for discussion.

passages.heading: Studio
passages.text: Supervised work with an emphasis on performance and creativity in which faculty instruct, assist, and critique.

passages.heading: Seminar
passages.text: Course offered to a small group (usually no more than 20 students) where participants actively exchange ideas and findings based on readings or research.

passages.heading: Independent Study
passages.text: One-on-one instruction in which the student enters into an agreement with the instructor that defines the focus of inquiry and nature of activities. Includes tutorials, directed readings, special projects.

passages.heading: Practicum
passages.text: Structured experiences where the primary aim is to connect theory with practice. Includes clinics, internships, externships, student teaching, field experiences. May include regular class meetings.

passages.heading: Workshop
passages.text: Similar to a seminar, with emphasis on applied rather than theoretical learning, but not offered for degree-program credit.

passages.heading: Major and Minor Changes
passages.text:
Major and Minor Changes
Tags: courses
Short Description: A distinction defined in Appendix E of the University Manual that identifies course changes requiring Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee review and those that do not.
Major and Minor Changes

passages.heading: Change the course description
passages.text: This only refers to the description of the course itself, and not to the sections which indicate the credits, method of instruction, prerequisites, grading method, etc.

passages.heading: Add or change a modality
passages.text:
Examples:
Adding an online version to an existing in-person course
Changing an existing in-person course to online-only (discontinuing the in-person offering)
Change the method of instruction
Change the course number to a new hundred level

passages.heading: Add general education outcomes to a course
passages.text:
Examples:
Adding General Education outcomes to a course that was not previously designated as a General Education course
Adding an additional General Education outcome to a course that currently has one General Education outcome
Changing a General Education outcome for a current General Education course

passages.heading: Add new topic to GCH course
passages.text:
Change the grading method of a general education course
Change number of fixed credits
Change fixed credits to a credit range
Change the credit range outside of the current range
Add graduate credit to a 400-level course

passages.heading: Minor Course Changes
passages.text:
Delete course
Change course title
Change academic home (department / college)
Remove a modality
Change prerequisites
Change subject code
Change cross-listing
Remove general education outcomes
Change temporary course to permanent
Change open ended topic course type (permanent topics vs temporary topics)
Change grading method of a non-GE course
Change course number within the hundred level
Change credit range inside of the current range
Change varied credits to fixed credits within current range
Change course repeat criteria
Remove graduate credit from a 400-level course
For more information, see Appendix E of the University Manual.

8.53.10 Student grades are defined as follows: A – Superior B – Good C – Fair D – Low grade, passing F – Failure 8.53.11 Grades shall be given quality point values as follows: A = 4.00 points A- = 3.70 points B+ = 3.30 points B = 3.00 points B- = 2.70 points C+ = 2.30 points C = 2.00 points C- = 1.70 points D+ = 1.30 points D = 1.00 points F = 0 points U = 0 points U* = not calculated in GPA

passages.heading: New Program Proposal Walkthrough
passages.text:
New Program Proposal Walkthrough
New Program Proposal Walkthrough
This guide provides step-by-step procedural instructions for completing and submitting a New Program Proposal in Kuali. It focuses on navigating the form, including what to select or enter in each field.
*In Kuali, Programs refer to Degrees, Majors, Minors & Certificates.
The guide is organized by proposal section (panel), so you can jump directly to a section when you need help.
This guide does not provide guidance on course content or academic decisions. Consult your department and applicable curriculum committees for questions about developing the course itself.
Navigate by Section
Related toolkit entry: Specialization Modification Proposal Walkthrough

passages.heading: Understand URI’s Curricular Process
passages.text:
Familiarize yourself with URI’s curricular process before beginning your proposal. This will help you understand the steps involved in the curricular process and accurately estimate how long your proposal may take to reach approval.
How the Curriculum Process Works

Approval Calendar

passages.heading: Make Sure You Can Access Kuali CM
passages.text:
You will need access to Kuali Curriculum Management (Kuali CM) to propose any curricular item.
Kuali Basics
Related toolkit entry: Kuali Basics

passages.heading: Start the Proposal
passages.text:
From your browser, navigate to Kuali Curriculum Management (CM).
Select Curriculum to open your Dashboard .
Related toolkit entry: Dashboard
From the left-hand navigation menu, select Programs.
On the Programs page, select + New Program in the upper-right corner.
The following sections of this walkthrough are grouped by section of the proposal form.

passages.heading: Contact Information
passages.text:
Complete the following fields with your contact information.
Proposer Name Your name is automatically populated based on your Kuali account.
Proposer Title Enter your university role.
Proposer Email Enter your URI email address. This is the email reviewers will use if they have questions about your proposal.
Additional Proposer(s) Use this section to identify additional individuals who can speak to the proposed program. Individuals listed here will not receive Kuali notifications or have access to edit the proposal. Their inclusion simply provides transparency to the reviewing committees about who else is involved in or can speak to the proposal.

passages.heading: Program Information
passages.text:
Effective Term & Year Select the term and year in which you intend the program to become effective. If the selected effective term has passed the applicable deadline by the time the proposal reaches the Faculty Senate, it will automatically be updated to the next available term.
First Graduation Term Select the term and year in which you anticipate the first students will graduate with this credential.
Credential Type Select the type of credential you are proposing: Degree, Major, Minor, or Certificate.
Level Select the level of the program: Undergraduate, Graduate, or Dual Currently, the only Dual Degree program offered at URI is the Pharm.D.
Academic Calendar Select the academic calendar for the program: Accelerated 7-week through URI Online, or Traditional 14-week with Summer and J-Term Sessions.
Program Locations Select all locations where the program will be offered.
College Select the college in which the program is housed.
Department Select the department in which the program is housed.
CIP Code Enter the specific CIP code that applies to your program. You can search for your program’s code here.

passages.heading: Program Information
passages.text:

passages.heading: Degree Requirements for the Bachelor’s Degree
passages.text:
Complete of a minimum of 120 credits (some majors require more)
Earn a minimum overall grade point average of 2.00 (some majors require a higher overall GPA)
Complete the coursework and other requirements for the curriculum of the major with the minimum grades per course and overall grade point averages for that major, or portions of that major, as specified in the section of the catalog which describes the requirements for each major
Complete General Education requirements, as specified elsewhere in this catalog
Abide by community standards as defined in the University Manual and Student Handbook
Complete the senior year in residence at URI
Earn one half of the total number of credits needed in the major at URI (same for a minor, if one is being pursued)
Transfer no more than half of the credits required for graduation from a two-year institution
Earn at least one-fourth of the credits required for graduation in-residence at URI (usually at least 30 credits)*
Students should review all major/degree requirements with their academic advisor to ensure completion of all course, credit and GPA minimums.

passages.heading: New Temporary & Permanent Course Email
passages.text:
New Temporary & Permanent Course Email
Date: May 31, 2027 (2027-05-31)
Tags: Temp Course Email
New Temporary & Permanent Course Email
The New Temporary & Permanent Course Email is distributed to all faculty, deans, and associate and assistant deans on the last weekday of each month. Recipients then have seven days to submit comments to the CASC Chair, GEC Chair, or Dean of the Graduate School regarding any potential or perceived content overlap involving a new temporary or permanent course.
The email serves two purposes:
Provides notice of upcoming Faculty Senate review. Courses included in the email have already been reviewed and approved by their respective College Curriculum Committees and will next be reviewed by the appropriate Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee: CASC, GEC, or Graduate Council.
Provides an opportunity to identify potential content overlap. College Curriculum Committees may review the courses included in the email to identify any potential or perceived overlap with courses offered or proposed by other colleges. Any concerns can then be raised before the courses proceed to Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee review.

passages.heading: Certification of New Courses by Originating Academic Unit
passages.text:
All new courses must be certified as having been reviewed by the faculty of the originating academic organization. Certification must be provided by the appropriate authority, which may include the Department Chair, Area Coordinator, or, in some cases, the College Curriculum Committee Chair.
The proposer should leave this section blank. The Department Chair or other authorized curriculum reviewer will complete the certification by checking the box to confirm that the course has been reviewed by the appropriate faculty, entering their name, and providing the date of certification.
Once the proposal reaches the course certification step in the workflow, it cannot move forward until the designated certifier completes this section.

passages.heading: The Approval Process
passages.text:
The curriculum approval process generally follows the sequence shown in the URI Curricular Approval Process Flowchart. Specific steps may vary by college, department, proposal type, and whether the proposal requires additional levels of review.
URI Curricular Approval Process Flowchart

passages.heading: Overview
passages.text:
Proposal Development Faculty use the forms in Kuali Curriculum Management to develop the proposal and work with other stakeholders as appropriate.
Department Review The proposal is reviewed through the appropriate departmental process.
College Curriculum Committee Review The College Curriculum Committee reviews the proposal.
College Dean Approval The College Dean approves the proposal for Faculty Senate review.
Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee Review The Curriculum & Standards Committee, the General Education Committee, or the Graduate Council reviews the proposal.
Faculty Senate Approval The Faculty Senate considers the curriculum committee's recommendation and votes.
University President Approval Any curricular item that is not a course must be reviewed and approved by the University President.
URI Board of Trustees Approval In addition to the University President’s approval, new Majors and Degrees are also reviewed by the Board of Trustees.

passages.heading: Workflows by College / Academic Group
passages.text: While all Colleges follow the curriculum approval process established in the University Manual, each College may have its own internal approval process based on its departmental and governance structures. To download a flowchart of a specific College’s approval process, select the College below.

passages.heading: Do I have to obtain a Library Impact Statement before submitting a proposal?
passages.text: No, the Library Impact Statement is completed within the Kuali proposal for all new courses, degrees, and majors, and is automatically routed to the Library Subject Selector to review and attach the LIS to the form.

passages.heading: Do I have to meet with the Learning Outcomes & Oversight Committee regarding my Assessment Plan prior to submitting my new degree, major, or certificate proposal?
passages.text:
No, you simply need to complete the appropriate assessment plan and attach it to the proposal. Once the proposal is submitted to the workflow, a notification is sent to the Associate Director of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment, and Accreditation, and members from the team will be in touch if any follow-up or revisions are necessary.

passages.text:
Program Description
Tags: programs
Short Description: The University Catalog description of an academic program, including its curriculum, degree requirements, and other requirements for completion.
Program Description
The University Catalog description of the requirements for completing an academic program, including the courses and credits required for the major, General Education, and free electives, as well as any additional program-specific requirements.

passages.heading: Degree and Major Description Formatting
passages.text:
Descriptive overview: A brief paragraph explaining the purpose of the program and the significance of the degree or major.
Specializations: The specializations (sub-plans) should be listed by name, but the requirements should not be listed in the program description.
Major Requirements: Listed, required courses
Professional Electives: Students choose from a list of courses selected specifically to align with the content of the program
Free Electives: Students are free to choose. Must provide a credit amount, minimum 6 credits for undergraduate degrees are required
Cumulative GPA and/or major GPA requirements
“A minimum GPA of 2.0 is required for graduation”
Total number of credits required to graduate
“A minimum of 120 credits is required for graduation”
Other Common Statements
“At least XX of all required courses for graduation must be numbered 300 and above”
“Students must earn a grade of X or better in all required courses”
“Students must complete a minimum of XX credits in the major”
“At least XX credits must be completed at the 300-level or above”
Total number of credits required to graduate (use the following phrase)
“A minimum of 120 credits is required for graduation”

passages.heading: Minor Description Formatting
passages.text:
Descriptive overview: A brief paragraph explaining the purpose and significance of the minor.
Course Requirements

passages.heading: Certificate Description Formatting

Total number of credits required to graduate

passages.heading: Degree or Major Program Requirements
passages.text:
An undergraduate student’s field of study is called the “major” (UM 8.20.40)
A graduate student’s field of study is called the “program” (UM 8.20.40)
Undergraduate programs are required to have a minimum or 120 credits, and a maximum of 148 (UM 8.21.10)
Undergraduate programs shall include at least 6 credits of free electives (UM 8.21.10)
General Education requirements shall apply to all undergraduate programs (UM 8.21.11)
A cumulative average of at least 2.00 is required to graduate from all undergraduate degrees. (UM 8.22.10)
Master’s degree programs with thesis require a minimum of 30 credits. 18 must be from content-based courses, 6 must be thesis courses. (GSM 7.44.1)
Master’s degree programs without thesis require a minimum of 30 credits. (GSM 7.45.1)
Doctoral students must complete a Program of Study with a minimum of 64 credit hours beyond the undergraduate degree (GSM 7.54) (See GSM sections 7.54 and 7.21)

passages.heading: Minor Requirements

18 or more credits of related studies offered by one or more departments or programs and sponsored by a faculty member. (UM 8.20.50)

Faculty Senate Meeting
Faculty Senate meetings are scheduled monthly from 3-5pm during the academic year. Sponsored receptions typically follow the meetings. These are great opportunities to build collegial relationships and network with colleagues from other disciplines. Special Meetings may be called upon due notice.
Meetings will be held in person at a pre-determined location on the Kinston Campus, as well as remotely on Zoom. Please check back to this page for up-to-date meeting locations and Zoom links. In September, December, and April, the General Faculty-Graduate Faculty Meeting directly precedes the Faculty Senate Meeting.
For more information, including zoom links and current and past Senate agendas, visit the Faculty Senate Meeting website.

passages.heading: Grand Challenge
passages.text:
Grand Challenge
Tags: courses
Short Description: A General Education overlay centered on a complex contemporary issue and designed to engage students through interdisciplinary perspectives and ethical inquiry.
Grand Challenge
A Grand Challenge course centers on a complex issue of contemporary significance and provides students with opportunities to explore, question, and critically engage with the issue. The course incorporates at least two disciplinary perspectives and helps students make interdisciplinary connections through assignments, activities, and/or experiences. It also addresses the ethical challenges associated with the issue, providing students with opportunities to apply ethical concepts or frameworks in evaluating potential actions and their ramifications.
Proposers will complete the Grand Challenge section in their Kuali Course Proposal. This Grand Challenge Template is available as a resource to help prepare responses for submission.

passages.heading: Kuali’s “Rules” Gadget
passages.text:
Kuali’s “Rules” Gadget
Kuali’s “Rules” Gadget
How to input Courses Approved for Double Counting in your ABM Specialization form.
Whether you are creating a new ABM, or modifying an existing, you will be asked to input all courses approved for double counting in a “Rules” gadget.

passages.heading: Adding Double-Counted Courses
passages.text:
Click Use Rule Categories checkbox
Click + Add Rules
In the blank box next to A, click the drop-down carrot, and select Double-Count.
In the next blank box, click the drop-down carrot, and select minimum number of credits from.
In the next blank box, click the drop-down carrot, and select selected courses.
Enter the total number of double-counted course credits in the Credits box. In the Courses box, list all courses that may be used toward these credits.
If the ABM allows only a certain number of credits from the courses specified, you can end here and move on to the next section of your form.

passages.heading: Adding Approved Course Statements
passages.text:
If you would like to add a statement indicating that other courses may be considered for double-counting with input from an advisor, program director, or other appropriate individual, follow these steps:
Click the plus (+) sign underneath the blue Update Logic button.
You will now see a blank box labeled with the letter B. In this box, click the drop-down carrot, and select Free form text.
Enter the text to accompany the courses selected.
Text Examples:
“Other 400-level ENG courses approved for graduate credit may be chosen in consultation with the program director.”
“Any 500-level CSF course approved by the advisor.”
“Nine credits may be double counted for the ABM Degree. Only 500­-level courses and 400­-level courses designated for graduate credit are eligible to be double counted.”

passages.heading: Credential Type

Credential Type
Tags: programs
Short Description: Identifies the type of academic credential awarded for a program. (Degree, Major, Minor, Certificate)
Credential Type

passages.heading: Degrees & Majors
passages.text:
The degree is the academic credential awarded by the University upon successful completion of an approved program of study and its associated requirements. Degrees may include bachelor's, master's, and doctoral degrees.
The major is the primary field of study within a degree program, consisting of a defined set of courses and requirements that students must complete.
University Manual 8.20.40 Major Fields of Study. An undergraduate student’s concentrated field of study in a degree-granting college shall be the student’s “major”; Fannon Institute students may have a “preferred major.” The major field of study for graduate students shall be the student’s “program.”

passages.heading: Degree / Major Program Requirements
passages.text:
Undergraduate programs are required to have a minimum or 120 credits, and a maximum of 148 (UM 8.21.10)
Undergraduate programs shall include at least 6 credits of free electives (UM 8.21.10)
General Education requirements shall apply to all undergraduate programs (UM 8.21.11)
A cumulative average of at least 2.00 is required to graduate from all undergraduate degrees. (UM 8.22.10)
Master’s degree programs with thesis require a minimum of 30 credits. 18 must be from content-based courses, 6 must be thesis courses. (GSM 7.44.1)
Master’s degree programs without thesis require a minimum of 30 credits. (GSM 7.45.1)
Doctoral students must complete a Program of Study with a minimum of 64 credit hours beyond the undergraduate degree (GSM 7.54) (See GSM sections 7.54 and 7.21)
In Kuali, the term program refers to all credential types; Degrees, majors, minors, and certificates. In the Manual, program refers to a graduate student’s major field of study.

passages.heading: Minor
passages.text:
A secondary concentration of undergraduate courses that provides students with a defined area of study outside their major. A minor generally requires 18 or more credits and is listed on the student’s permanent academic record after graduation.
University Manual 8.20.50 Minor Fields of Study. Undergraduate Students may declare a “minor” field of study. A minor is a secondary concentration of courses.

Minimum GPA average of 2.0 must be earned in the minor’s required courses (UM 8.20.51)
A maximum of two courses can apply to both the major and minor field of study (UM 8.20.52)

passages.heading: Method of Instruction
passages.text:
Method of Instruction
Tags: courses
Short Description: The instructional delivery method. Also known as "class component.”
Method of Instruction
Provided below is the complete list of approved methods of instruction, as proposed in FSEC Report #2024-2025-03 and subsequently approved by the Faculty Senate through Bill #24-25-12 on January 23, 2025.

passages.heading: Lecture
passages.text: A course in which the primary method is presentation and students are expected to participate in a variety of ways, such as small-group discussions, questions and answers, writing-exercises, etc.

passages.heading: Laboratory
passages.text: Applied course work, generally involving experimentation or observation, typically using special equipment (including computers and specialized software).

passages.heading: Recitation
passages.text: Separate sections of a lecture course regularly scheduled for discussion.

passages.heading: Studio
passages.text: Supervised work with an emphasis on performance and creativity in which faculty instruct, assist, and critique.

passages.heading: Seminar
passages.text: Course offered to a small group (usually no more than 20 students) where participants actively exchange ideas and findings based on readings or research.

passages.heading: Independent Study
passages.text: One-on-one instruction in which the student enters into an agreement with the instructor that defines the focus of inquiry and nature of activities. Includes tutorials, directed readings, special projects.

passages.heading: Practicum
passages.text: Structured experiences where the primary aim is to connect theory with practice. Includes clinics, internships, externships, student teaching, field experiences. May include regular class meetings.

passages.heading: Workshop
passages.text: Similar to a seminar, with emphasis on applied rather than theoretical learning, but not offered for degree-program credit.
